ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The left side of the figure is the primary side of the transformer, connected with an AC power supply symbol and an ammeter A; the right side is the secondary-side circuit. On the upper side of the secondary side, a resistor R is first connected in series, and then reaches a node. From this node downward there is bulb L1, connected to the bottom loop; on the right there is also a branch, with switch S on the upper part of the branch and bulb L2 on the lower part, and the whole is connected in parallel with the branch where L1 is located. The problem states that S is initially open, and the primary-side AC voltage is stable. Reasoning: When S is open, the secondary-side load is mainly the series equivalent relationship of R and L1; if at some moment S is closed, then L2 is connected in and becomes an additional load in parallel with L1, making the equivalent load resistance after R decrease. The total current on the secondary side increases, and the current flowing through the series resistor R increases, so the voltage drop across R increases. Since the induced voltage on the secondary side is determined by the stable primary-side voltage and is basically stable, after more voltage is divided across R, the voltage across L1 decreases, so L1 will become slightly dimmer. Therefore, the change that can explain this phenomenon is that switch S is closed.

method.method_draft: First identify the secondary-side topology in the image: R is in series with the load section, L1 is already connected, and S would connect L2 as an additional parallel load. From the text, the primary AC voltage is stable and S starts open. If S is closed, L2 is added to the secondary load, so the equivalent resistance after R decreases. The secondary current through R increases, making the voltage drop on R larger. Thus the terminal voltage across L1 falls, so L1 becomes slightly dimmer. Therefore the change explaining the observation is that switch S was closed.
